TV pictures showed distraught mourners crowding and reaching out to the coffins as they were carried aloft. Several people were seen to collapse and had to be carried away. Mourners also carried photographs, threw rose petals and unfurled banners, some of which read "We Won't Kneel," AP said. The coffins were greeted at the Christian Maronite church with applause from the gathered mourners, the agency said, including majority leaders and the Lebanese cabinet as well as Ghanem's family and friends. Ghanem was later buried in the city's Christian district. Ghanem's death is the latest in a series of attacks targeting prominent anti-Syrian figures, with the most notorious being the February 2005 assassination in Beirut of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, which sparked widespread protests that led to the ouster of Syrian forces from Lebanon. Hariri also died in a massive explosion. The incident threatens to cast the country into political uncertainty ahead of a key presidential vote in a tightly divided parliament, almost evenly split between anti- and pro-Syrian camps.  Watch how Ghanem's death disrupts Lebanese politics » . CNN's Beirut bureau chief Brent Sadler said that many Lebanese now feared for the future, especially given other events in the region including the conflict between Palestinians and Israelis, recent political differences in Iraq and Iran's bid to become a super power. Also in a written statement, a spokesperson for Ban Ki-moon said the U.N. secretary-general "condemns in the strongest terms this terrorist attack." "The secretary general urges all Lebanese to exercise utmost calm and restraint at this very critical time and to allow judicial procedures to take their course," the spokesperson said. Bush's statement added: "The United States opposes any attempts to intimidate the Lebanese people as they seek to exercise their democratic right to select a president without foreign interference. We will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Lebanese people as they resist attempts by the Syrian and Iranian regimes and their allies to destabilize Lebanon and undermine its sovereignty." The U.S. Embassy in Beirut issued a statement saying: "It is not a coincidence that these attacks target those figures who have been working to secure Lebanon's independence from renewed Syrian hegemony. We note with concern that many Lebanese politicians allied with Syria have in fact warned that murder and violence would be the results of any effort to exercise genuine parliamentary democracy." And U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, in a written statement, said: "The bombing that claimed these lives was another act in a campaign of terror by those who want to turn back the clock on Lebanon's hard-won democratic gains." "The world should speak with one voice in calling for an end to violence in Lebanon intended to subvert democratic processes in that country," Rice said. "Lebanese elections, scheduled to begin in just days, must proceed, in accordance with the Constitution, without threats of foreign interference and the violence that accompanies such obstruction." # Lebanon mourns slain lawmaker after Beirut assassination

**BEIRUT, Lebanon** — Thousands of mourners gathered in Beirut on Friday for the funeral of Lebanese parliament member Antoine Ghanem, an anti-Syrian lawmaker killed in a car bombing that deepened Lebanon’s political crisis and drew condemnation from U.S. and U.N. officials.

Ghanem, a member of the Christian Phalange Party and part of Lebanon’s Western-backed parliamentary majority, was assassinated Wednesday in an explosion in a Christian neighborhood of the Lebanese capital. Several others were also killed in the blast, which tore through vehicles and storefronts and left residents fearing a return to the political violence that has shaken the country in recent years.

His coffin, draped in the Lebanese flag, was carried through crowds of supporters, party members and political allies. Many mourners waved Lebanese flags and chanted slogans against political violence and foreign interference. Church bells rang as religious and political leaders attended funeral services for the slain legislator.

Ghanem’s death came just days before Lebanon’s parliament was expected to begin the process of choosing a successor to President Emile Lahoud, a pro-Syrian figure whose term was nearing its end. His killing reduced the already slim margin held by the ruling anti-Syrian coalition in parliament, heightening fears that assassinations were being used to influence the presidential vote.

Lebanon’s governing coalition blamed the attack on forces seeking to destabilize the country and weaken the parliamentary majority. Opposition figures denied involvement and also condemned the killing.

The assassination was the latest in a series of attacks targeting prominent Lebanese politicians, journalists and security officials, many of them critics of Syrian influence in Lebanon. Former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri was killed in a massive Beirut bombing in 2005, an attack that triggered widespread protests and led to the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon after nearly three decades.

U.S. officials strongly condemned Ghanem’s assassination and expressed support for Lebanon’s government. President George W. Bush and Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice both described the killing as an attack on Lebanon’s democracy and sovereignty. Washington urged Lebanese leaders to proceed with constitutional processes despite intimidation and violence.

The United Nations also condemned the bombing. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called for those responsible to be brought to justice and said the attack underscored the need to protect Lebanon’s democratic institutions. Members of the U.N. Security Council similarly denounced the assassination and warned against attempts to destabilize the country.

As mourners filled the streets, Lebanese leaders appealed for unity, but the atmosphere remained tense. Security forces were deployed across parts of Beirut, and many residents expressed fear that more violence could follow as the presidential election approached.

Ghanem had only recently returned to Lebanon after spending time abroad because of security concerns. Like several other members of the parliamentary majority, he had been considered at risk because of his political stance.

For many at the funeral, his death was not only a personal loss but a sign of Lebanon’s continuing struggle over power, sovereignty and the legacy of Syrian influence.

## News Report: Lebanon Buries MP Antoine Ghanem Amid Mass Mourning and Renewed Political Crisis

**Beirut, Lebanon —** Lebanon held a highly charged funeral and burial for **Antoine Ghanem**, a Christian member of parliament from the **Kataeb Party** and the anti-Syrian **March 14 coalition**, following his assassination in a car bombing that deepened the country’s political crisis and heightened fears of renewed instability.

Ghanem was killed on **19 September 2007** in a powerful explosion in the Beirut suburb of **Sin el-Fil**, a predominantly Christian area. The blast also killed several other people, including members of his entourage, and wounded many bystanders. His funeral drew thousands of mourners, political leaders, clergy, party supporters, and ordinary citizens who gathered to pay respects and to denounce what they described as an attack on Lebanon’s sovereignty and democratic institutions.

### Public Mourning and Funeral Scenes

The burial ceremonies took place in an atmosphere of grief mixed with anger. Lebanese flags, Kataeb Party banners, black mourning ribbons, and portraits of Ghanem were displayed along roads and near the church where funeral rites were held. Crowds applauded, wept, and chanted slogans as his coffin passed through the streets, reflecting both personal mourning and political defiance.

Many mourners described Ghanem’s killing as part of a broader campaign targeting anti-Syrian figures in Lebanon. His coffin, draped in the Lebanese flag, was received by relatives, party colleagues, and supporters. Church bells tolled as religious leaders led prayers, while security forces maintained a heavy presence around the funeral route and nearby political sites.

The funeral was also marked by the presence of prominent March 14 leaders, including senior figures from the Kataeb Party, the Lebanese Forces, the Future Movement, and other anti-Syrian factions. Their attendance turned the burial into both a national mourning event and a political rally.

### Who Was Antoine Ghanem?

Antoine Ghanem was a Maronite Christian lawmaker affiliated with the **Kataeb Party**, one of Lebanon’s oldest Christian political movements. He was part of the parliamentary majority aligned with the **March 14 alliance**, the coalition that emerged after the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister **Rafik Hariri** and the subsequent withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon.

Ghanem had recently returned to Lebanon from abroad. Like several other March 14 politicians, he had spent time outside the country or under tightened security because of threats against anti-Syrian lawmakers. His death shocked supporters, in part because it showed that even heightened precautions had not ended the campaign of assassinations.

### Political Implications

Ghanem’s killing carried major political consequences. At the time, Lebanon was approaching a critical **presidential election** to choose a successor to President **Émile Lahoud**, whose term was due to end in November 2007. The country was already deeply divided between the March 14 parliamentary majority and the opposition led by **Hezbollah**, the Amal Movement, and the Free Patriotic Movement.

The assassination reduced the number of March 14 MPs and intensified concerns that the parliamentary majority was being physically weakened ahead of the vote. Several March 14 lawmakers had already been assassinated or targeted since 2005, including **Gebran Tueni**, **Pierre Gemayel**, and **Walid Eido**. Ghanem’s death reinforced fears that killings were being used to alter the balance of power in parliament.

March 14 leaders blamed Syria or pro-Syrian forces for the assassination, arguing that the killing fit a pattern of attacks against politicians, journalists, and security officials who opposed Syrian influence in Lebanon. Damascus denied involvement, as it had in previous cases.

### A Country on Edge

The burial came at a time when Lebanon was experiencing severe institutional paralysis. The cabinet of Prime Minister **Fouad Siniora** was contested by the opposition, parliament was frequently deadlocked, and rival political camps accused each other of undermining the state. The assassination heightened fears that Lebanon could return to the kind of political violence that had marked earlier periods of its history.

Security was increased across Beirut and other sensitive areas. Many politicians limited their movements, while some MPs were reportedly staying in guarded hotels or undisclosed locations to reduce the risk of further attacks.

### March 14’s Message

At the funeral, March 14 figures portrayed Ghanem as a “martyr” for Lebanese independence. Speeches emphasized themes of sovereignty, resistance to intimidation, and the need to proceed with the presidential election despite violence.

For the March 14 coalition, the assassination was not only a personal loss but also a warning. Leaders argued that the killing was meant to frighten MPs, disrupt the election, and prevent the emergence of a president aligned with the parliamentary majority. They vowed not to abandon the political process.

### Broader Significance

Antoine Ghanem’s burial symbolized the fragile state of Lebanon in 2007: a country still grieving the assassinations that followed Rafik Hariri’s death, still divided over Syria’s role, and still struggling to maintain functioning institutions under intense pressure.

His killing deepened sectarian and political anxieties, particularly among Christian communities aligned with March 14, and intensified international concern over Lebanon’s stability. Western and Arab governments condemned the assassination and called for restraint, while Lebanese leaders warned that the country was facing a deliberate campaign to destabilize its democracy.

In the end, Ghanem’s funeral was more than a burial. It was a public expression of grief, fear, anger, and political resolve — a moment that captured Lebanon’s precarious balance between mourning and confrontation.

The blast, which tore through a busy residential and commercial district, also killed several other people and wounded many more, reviving memories of the wave of political assassinations that has shaken the country since the 2005 killing of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri.

On Friday, mourners carrying Lebanese flags and Phalange Party banners gathered outside churches and along major roads leading to central Beirut. Many wept openly as Ghanem’s coffin, draped in the red-and-white Lebanese flag, was carried through the crowd. Church bells rang as supporters chanted slogans against political violence and foreign interference, while party officials and members of the governing March 14 coalition vowed that the killing would not derail their effort to elect a new president.

The funeral quickly became more than a rite of mourning. It was a demonstration by Lebanon’s anti-Syrian camp, which has steadily lost members of parliament to assassination since the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon in 2005. Ghanem’s death further narrowed the majority’s margin in Parliament and heightened fears that political killings are being used to alter the balance of power ahead of a crucial presidential vote.

“This is not only a funeral for Antoine Ghanem,” one mourner said near the procession route. “It is a funeral for every Lebanese person who wants to live without fear.”

Ghanem, a veteran politician from the Metn district and a senior member of the Phalange Party, was widely seen as a loyal figure within the March 14 alliance, the bloc that emerged after Hariri’s assassination to demand Syrian withdrawal and sovereignty for Lebanon. His killing came as Parliament was preparing to convene to choose a successor to President Émile Lahoud, a pro-Syrian figure whose term was due to end in November amid a bitter standoff between the Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition.

The timing of the assassination has intensified accusations from March 14 leaders that the murders of anti-Syrian lawmakers are part of a campaign to intimidate the majority and prevent it from securing the presidency. Opposition leaders have rejected such charges and called for unity, but the political atmosphere remains deeply poisoned.

Lebanon’s presidential election is rarely a simple domestic contest. Under the country’s confessional power-sharing system, the presidency is reserved for a Maronite Christian, the premiership for a Sunni Muslim and the speakership of Parliament for a Shiite Muslim. But the office of president has long been tied to broader regional influence — historically involving Syria, and more recently reflecting the rivalry among Damascus, Tehran, Riyadh, Washington and Paris.

The immediate crisis centers on whether the governing coalition and opposition can agree on a consensus candidate, or whether the March 14 majority will attempt to elect a president on its own. The opposition has warned that any president chosen without broad agreement would be illegitimate, while government leaders say they have a constitutional right and a national duty to ensure the office is not left vacant.

Ghanem’s assassination has made that already fragile process even more perilous.

In speeches delivered during the funeral ceremonies, March 14 figures linked Ghanem’s death to the unresolved legacy of Hariri’s assassination, which marked a turning point in Lebanon’s modern history. Hariri, a billionaire businessman and former prime minister credited with leading much of Beirut’s post-civil-war reconstruction, was killed on February 14, 2005, when a massive explosion struck his motorcade along the capital’s seafront.

Hariri’s death triggered enormous demonstrations known as the Cedar Revolution, bringing hundreds of thousands of Lebanese into the streets to demand the end of Syria’s nearly three-decade military presence in Lebanon. Under international and domestic pressure, Syrian troops withdrew in April 2005. But the withdrawal did not bring stability. Instead, Lebanon entered a prolonged period of confrontation between the March 14 coalition and factions aligned with Syria and Iran, including Hezbollah and its allies.

Since Hariri’s killing, a succession of journalists, security officials and politicians critical of Syria have been assassinated or targeted in bombings. Among those killed were journalist Samir Kassir, former Communist Party leader George Hawi, lawmaker and newspaper executive Gebran Tueni, Industry Minister Pierre Gemayel and MP Walid Eido. Each assassination deepened a sense among many Lebanese that political murder had returned as a tool of power.

The investigation into Hariri’s assassination led to the creation of an international tribunal, strongly backed by the March 14 coalition and opposed by Syria and its allies, who denied involvement and accused the tribunal’s supporters of politicizing justice. The tribunal became one of the central flashpoints in Lebanese politics, widening the divide between the government of Prime Minister Fouad Siniora and the opposition.

That divide had already pushed the country into institutional crisis. Hezbollah and allied ministers resigned from Siniora’s cabinet in 2006, arguing that the government no longer reflected Lebanon’s sectarian balance. The government rejected that claim and continued to operate, while opposition supporters staged a prolonged sit-in in downtown Beirut, paralyzing the capital’s commercial heart.

The 2006 war between Hezbollah and Israel further complicated Lebanon’s political landscape. While Hezbollah emerged among its supporters claiming resistance and survival, its opponents accused it of dragging Lebanon into a devastating conflict without state approval. Reconstruction, security and the question of Hezbollah’s weapons remained unresolved, adding to tensions around the presidential succession.

Against that backdrop, Ghanem’s murder landed like a warning.

Security was heavy across Beirut on Friday, with army units and internal security forces deployed near churches, government buildings and major intersections. Soldiers inspected vehicles, blocked side streets and stood watch from armored personnel carriers as mourners gathered. Despite the visible security presence, many Lebanese expressed frustration that assassins had repeatedly managed to strike prominent figures in the capital and its suburbs.

The bombing that killed Ghanem was the latest reminder of how vulnerable Lebanon’s political class remains. The explosion occurred in a crowded area of east Beirut, a predominantly Christian part of the city considered friendly territory for the anti-Syrian majority. Witnesses described a huge fireball, mangled cars and shattered storefronts. Television images showed rescue workers carrying bloodied victims through smoke and debris.

At the funeral, anger mixed with anxiety. Some mourners spoke of a plot to reduce the parliamentary majority one death at a time. Others feared that further assassinations could push the country toward renewed civil strife. Lebanon’s 1975-1990 civil war remains an ever-present memory, and political leaders frequently warn that the country’s sectarian divisions could again turn violent if institutions collapse.

Yet even as they accused unnamed enemies of seeking to break their coalition, March 14 leaders urged supporters to remain peaceful and focused on the presidential election.

“We will elect a president,” one speaker declared to applause. “We will defend the republic.”

The challenge is that Lebanon’s republic is deeply divided over what kind of president it should have. March 14 wants a head of state clearly committed to sovereignty, the international tribunal and limiting Syrian influence. The opposition insists on a consensus president who will not align Lebanon with Western pressure or move against Hezbollah’s weapons. Between those positions lies a narrow path that foreign mediators have struggled to widen.

France, the United States, Saudi Arabia and Egypt have all watched the presidential deadline with concern. Syria, though formally absent militarily since 2005, remains a central actor in Lebanese calculations. Iran’s support for Hezbollah adds another regional layer. For many Lebanese, the presidency has become a test of whether the country can make decisions through its own institutions or remains an arena for proxy conflict.

Ghanem’s death has also revived fears over parliamentary arithmetic. Lebanon’s 128-member legislature was already polarized, and the governing bloc’s majority had been reduced by previous assassinations. If enough anti-Syrian lawmakers were killed or intimidated from attending, the majority’s ability to elect a president could be threatened. Several MPs from the coalition have spent long periods outside Lebanon or under heavy security, fearing assassination.

Ghanem himself had reportedly returned to the country only shortly before the bombing. His supporters said that fact made his death especially chilling: even absence abroad offered no lasting protection, and returning to fulfill parliamentary duties could be fatal.

As the funeral procession moved through Beirut, portraits of Ghanem were held aloft alongside images of other slain figures from the March 14 movement. For many in the crowd, the faces formed a grim political ledger — Hariri, Tueni, Gemayel, Eido, and now Ghanem — each name marking another stage in Lebanon’s unresolved battle over power, justice and sovereignty.

At the center of that battle remains the legacy of Rafik Hariri. To his supporters, Hariri symbolized Lebanon’s postwar revival and its aspiration to rejoin the Arab and international mainstream after years of Syrian domination. To his critics, he represented a political and economic order that enriched elites and left the country burdened by debt. But his assassination undeniably transformed Lebanon, redrawing alliances and making the demand for accountability a defining issue.

The international investigation into Hariri’s killing, and later the tribunal process, became a rallying point for March 14 and a source of suspicion for its opponents. The debate over justice was never separate from the debate over power. Ghanem’s assassination has now reinforced the belief among many government supporters that the campaign of killings is intended to prevent Lebanon from completing the political transition that began after Hariri’s death.

Still, the country’s divisions were visible even in the calls for unity. Opposition leaders condemned the assassination, but pro-government figures treated those condemnations with skepticism. Many Lebanese citizens, exhausted by years of crisis, said they feared all sides would use the killing to harden their positions rather than compromise.

In Beirut’s neighborhoods, daily life continued under the shadow of uncertainty. Cafés were open, traffic pushed through security bottlenecks and shopkeepers swept broken glass from previous days’ disturbances. But conversations returned again and again to the same questions: Who would be next? Would Parliament meet? Could the presidency be settled peacefully? And would another assassination tip the country into a wider confrontation?

For Ghanem’s family and supporters, those questions were secondary on Friday to the immediate pain of burial. Inside the church, clergy offered prayers for the dead and for Lebanon, invoking a country that has too often mourned its leaders violently. Outside, the crowd answered with chants of loyalty and grief.

By afternoon, as the coffin was taken toward its final resting place, the mood remained tense but controlled. Political leaders departed under heavy guard. Mourners lingered in clusters, some embracing, others staring silently at posters of the slain MP.

Lebanon has endured many such funerals, and each has carried the same promise from the living: that the death will not be in vain. But Ghanem’s assassination comes at a particularly dangerous hour, with the presidency unresolved, Parliament under threat and the country’s rival camps locked in a confrontation that neither side appears able to win outright.

For now, the streets of Beirut have absorbed another day of mourning. The larger test — whether Lebanon’s leaders can prevent that mourning from becoming another step toward institutional collapse — lies just ahead.
